narrative:
Based on the assessment, there is a 22% chance you will fail your final year. While this may not seem high, it exceeds the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for remedial courses — a precautionary measure designed to support students before difficulties become serious.

Three factors most strongly shaped this prediction, and importantly, all three actually worked in your favor, reducing your predicted risk of failing.

The most influential factor was your history of past failures — you have none. This is a strong positive signal, as students who have previously struggled academically are at considerably higher risk. Your clean record meaningfully lowered your predicted risk.

The second most important factor was your ambition to pursue higher education. Every student not required to take remedial courses shares this goal, and your motivation to continue studying beyond school is a genuine protective factor that the assessment recognized.

Third, your weekly study time of 2 to 5 hours also contributed positively. Most students not required to take remedial courses study at least this much, with a third studying even more. Your current habits are reasonable, though increasing your study time could further reduce your risk.

Despite these positive signals, your overall risk remains above the safety threshold, likely due to a combination of other background factors. The remedial courses are not a punishment — they are a proactive support measure. Attending them, maintaining your zero-absence record, and ideally increasing your weekly study hours will give you the best possible chance of finishing your final year successfully.
